triageSets.title: On the road
triageSets.brief: You're working away from the depot and the public networks and sign-in pages keep coming up: a café's Wi-Fi list, a hotel's, a page that wants your work password, a notice about a lost device. For each one, choose Trust (you'd connect or carry on), Report, Delete, or Verify (ask the venue for the network's name, or ring the service desk). On the venue's own network, with the VPN, ordinary work is fine; a page that wants your work password, or a network named to look like the venue's, is the trap. Never type your work password into a Wi-Fi page. Reporting or checking when you're unsure is always fine and never marked down, and no real network is joined and no real password is typed here.
triageSets._labels: The set holds Wi-Fi network lists, sign-in pages and emails, so the engine's default verdict hints ('This is real. I'd open it or act on it', 'This is a phish. Send it to security') and the 'Inbox check: N messages' queue heading read as email. labels.verdict.<v>.hint rewords the four hints to fit a network, a page or a message, and labels.queue.inbox relabels the brief heading ('On the road: N networks, pages and messages'). The four button LABELS stay Trust/Report/Delete/Verify, which the set brief glosses ('Trust (you'd connect or carry on)', 'Verify (ask the venue...)'); a single relabel can't fit networks, pages and emails at once (playtest F-E20-1, 2026-10-29).

trust.hint: This one's safe. I'd connect or carry on.

report.hint: This is a fake or a trap. Tell security.

verify.hint: I'd check first: ask the venue, or ring a number I already hold.

messages._note: Card 1. The genuine Wi-Fi list (page.state wifiList), the 'you can trust the venue's own network' half of the set. At The Bean and Barrow a chalkboard by the till names the guest network, so the right move is Trust (join the board-named network and let the VPN come up) or Verify (ask staff to confirm the name); under the awareness profile a cautious Report or Verify still scores full. There is deliberately NO look-alike of the café's name in this list: the stronger neighbour 'The Daily Grind' is a different venue, not a BeanBarrow look-alike, so there is no lookalike_network flag to tick here. B1 M1 fix (2026-10-29): an earlier version put 'BeanBarrow Free' in this genuine list, so Trust and Report both scored 100 and ticking the look-alike chip read 'Not a flag here'; the list now carries one clear answer. The look-alike-network lesson is carried by card 2 (Haverbridge).
messages.subject: At The Bean and Barrow: the Wi-Fi list
messages.body: You're after a seat and a coffee, and you open the Wi-Fi list to get online. Trust here means joining the network the café names.

page.venueNote: The chalkboard by the till names the guest network 'BeanBarrow Guest'.

networks.note: The name written up on the chalkboard by the till

whyFine.default: The board names the café's network, so you are not guessing: join 'BeanBarrow Guest', let the VPN come up, and ordinary work on it is fine. A stronger signal from a differently named network, like 'The Daily Grind' next door, is not yours. Asking staff to confirm the name does the same job.

truth.falseAlarmCost: Reported instead of joined, you spend the afternoon on your phone's data and the VPN never comes up, over a network the café's own staff named on the board.

messages._note: Card 2. The look-alike half of the mirror pair. A Wi-Fi network list (page.state wifiList) at Haverbridge Lodge with no staff sign, where a stronger 'Haverbridge Lodge FREE' sits next to 'Haverbridge Lodge Guest' and is already selected. The scenario-local lookalike_network tell lives here. Correct move Report (don't just pick the strongest; ask the front desk for the name, or use the phone's hotspot).
messages.subject: At Haverbridge Lodge: the Wi-Fi list
messages.body: You've checked in and you open the Wi-Fi list in your room.

page.venueNote: No sign names the Wi-Fi here, and the strongest network is already selected for you.

lookalike_network.redFlag: A public Wi-Fi network named to look like the venue's, often with a stronger signal

truth.kindLine: This network was named to look like the hotel's; it wasn't the real one.

perFlagNote.lookalike_network: 'Haverbridge Lodge FREE', in capitals with the strongest signal, sits right next to 'Haverbridge Lodge Guest'. Anyone can name a hotspot to look like the venue's, and a stronger signal says nothing about who runs it.

truth.ifTrusted: Joining it would run your traffic through whoever set it up, and the sign-in page it opens is the next step of the trap.
truth.reportReply: Thanks. With no sign to tell you the real name, the move is to ask the front desk, or use your phone's hotspot, never to pick the strongest signal. Reporting it warns the next guest.

messages._note: Card 3. The over-asking Wi-Fi sign-in page (built page kind, padlock false so the bar shows 'Not secure'; nothing typeable). On tarrowby-wifi.example (reused E6 look-alike). Asks for the work email and password to get online. The scenario-local wifi_page_credentials tell lives here. Cross-references E5 (the padlock myth) in the perFlagNote so the two episodes do not contradict. Correct move Report. Supporting contrast to card 4.
messages.subject: From the Wi-Fi: 'Sign in to get online'
messages.body: Sign in with your work account to get free Wi-Fi.

autofillNote.none: Your password manager did not fill this in, because it does not recognise the page.

wifi_page_credentials.redFlag: A Wi-Fi sign-in page asking for your work password, or for more than accepting the terms

truth.kindLine: This page was a fake, after your work password; a real Wi-Fi page never needs it.

perFlagNote.wifi_page_credentials: A venue's Wi-Fi page asks you to accept the terms, sometimes an email or a room number. It has no reason to want your work password; one that does is a fake. The bar here also reads 'Not secure'. Even with a padlock, no Wi-Fi page needs your work password: a padlock only means the connection is encrypted, not that the page is honest.

truth.ifTrusted: Your work email and password would go to whoever put the page up, and they could sign in as you from anywhere.
truth.reportReply: Thanks. No Wi-Fi page needs your work password. Close it, join the network the venue names or use your phone's hotspot, and report the page.

messages._note: Card 4. The genuine captive portal (built page kind, no new state). On thebeanandbarrow.example, a single 'I accept the terms' tick and a Connect button, no password box and so no autofill cue. Correct move Trust (carry on). The genuine contrast to card 3: a Wi-Fi page appearing is not itself the tell; what it asks for is.
messages.subject: From the café Wi-Fi: accept and connect
messages.body: Welcome to The Bean and Barrow. Tick to accept the terms and connect.

page.heading: The Bean and Barrow free Wi-Fi

whyFine.wifi_page_credentials: It asks for no password, just the terms. A Wi-Fi page turning up is not the tell; what it asks for is.
whyFine.default: A real venue page asks you to accept the terms and nothing more. Tick and connect, and let the VPN cover the rest.

truth.falseAlarmCost: Reported instead of accepted, you never get on the café's Wi-Fi and spend the afternoon on your phone's data, over a page that only asked you to tick a box.

messages._note: Card 5. The genuine lost-device reminder (built email kind). From Tarrowby's IT service desk on the real domain, asking for nothing and naming the usual route. Correct move Trust (and act on it: keep the number to hand). The lock buys time; reporting at once is what lets them lock, wipe and sign the device out. Supporting contrast to card 6.
messages.subject: If you lose a work device, ring us straight away
messages.body:
A reminder for everyone on the road: if you lose a work phone, tablet or laptop, ring the 24/7 service desk straight away, day or night, even if it's locked and even if you think it'll turn up. Tell us what it was, when and where you last had it, and what was on it. We can lock or wipe it, but only once you tell us. We'll never ask for your password.
The IT Service Desk

whyFine.default: A genuine reminder from the service desk on Tarrowby's own address, asking for nothing and naming the usual route. The lock buys time; reporting at once is what lets them lock, wipe and sign the device out. Keep the 24/7 number to hand.

truth.falseAlarmCost: Reported as if it were a scam, you might not save the one number that matters when a device actually goes missing, and the hours before you ring are the ones that count.

messages._note: Card 6. The one lure in the set: a lost-device sign-in lure (built email kind), a core_09 topic that neither E6 nor E10 covers. 'Device Recovery' on the reused look-alike tarrowbey.example offers to locate your device if you sign in within 24 hours. The scenario-local found_device_lure tell lives here, alongside the shared lookalike_domain tell. Correct move Report. You find a lost device by ringing the service desk, never by signing in to a link that found you first.
messages.subject: We've detected your lost work device

found_device_lure.redFlag: A message offering to locate or recover a lost device if you sign in

truth.kindLine: This was a fake lost-device message, after your work password; it wasn't from the service desk.

perFlagNote.found_device_lure: You find a lost device by ringing the service desk, never by signing in to a message that found you first. The 24-hour clock is there to rush you past that thought.
perFlagNote.lookalike_domain: The address is tarrowbey.example, not tarrowby.example: a look-alike with an added letter. The 'Locate my device' link goes to a sign-in page on that same look-alike.

truth.ifTrusted: The link opens a sign-in page that takes your work password; nothing is ever located.
truth.reportReply: Thanks. The service desk doesn't email you to locate a device, and tarrowbey.example isn't ours. You report lost kit by ringing the desk, day or night.

awarenessEpisode.scopeNote: Authorised exercise at Tarrowby Logistics, a fictional company. In scope: the everyday choices you make working away from the office, and the public networks and sign-in pages you sort afterwards. No real network is joined and no real password is ever typed; every network, page, venue and message is made up.

strings.brief: You're on an authorised exercise at Tarrowby Logistics, a fictional haulier. First you spend two days working away from the depot, and make five everyday calls on the road: on the train, in the café and its queue, and when a tablet goes missing. You make each call, then you see where it led. After that you sort the safe networks and pages from the look-alikes, a hotel's among them. Only that last part is scored. Nothing you tap is a real network, and no real password is ever typed.
strings.noBlameLine: Reading a screen over someone's shoulder, joining a network named like the café, or leaving a bag for a minute are ordinary slips that happen to careful people; the harm is in the hours before anyone says so, not in the slip. A miss here just shows what to change.
strings.teamLine: By reporting or checking {n} of these rather than acting on them, you kept a trap away from the rest of your team.
strings.mondayCard: On Monday, three things: turn on the screen lock and auto-lock on your own phone if they're not on already; set your devices to forget public Wi-Fi networks and turn off auto-join, so they don't rejoin a look-alike by themselves; and save the 24/7 service desk number in your phone, so if you lose a work device you can report it on the spot. Report anything at work using the route in the box below.
strings.defendOnly: A look-alike network, or a page after your work password, catches careful people on the road. Any you were caught out by are shown below, with what gives each one away.
strings._conceptPanel: B1 m4 (2026-10-29): this fragment carries the DEFEND-ONLY concept set, the four panels that match what the sort itself covers (public Wi-Fi, the look-alike and over-asking page, the lost device, Tarrowby's controls). The full-episode 'Out of sight, out of earshot' and 'At home, mind the camera' panels are dropped here because the defend-only learner never sees the train/queue/home scenes they summarise; they stay in the FULL erb's conceptPanel (six panels). conceptPanel value is allow-listed to differ between fragment and full erb (social-awareness-fragment-erb-parity.test.mjs STRINGS_VALUE_EXEMPT), and the generator copies this fragment set into the defend-only shell.

conceptPanel.heading: Public Wi-Fi, in proportion
conceptPanel.text: Nearly everything you do now is encrypted, and Tarrowby's laptops add a VPN (a secure tunnel back to the company) on top, so ordinary work on the venue's own network is mostly fine. The old 'anyone on the café Wi-Fi can read your email' is out of date. What still catches people is a network named to look like the venue's, and a page that asks for your work password.

conceptPanel.heading: The look-alike and the over-asking page
conceptPanel.text: You can't tell who runs a hotspot, so ask the venue for the network's name, and don't just pick the strongest signal. A venue's page asks you to accept the terms, sometimes an email or a room number. It never needs your work password; if one asks, close it, use your phone's hotspot, and report it.

conceptPanel.heading: With you, or locked away. Lost it? Report it now
conceptPanel.text: A device never sits unattended in a café, a train or a car, even for two minutes. If you lose one, ring the service desk straight away, day or night, even if it's locked: the lock buys time, and the hours before you report are what matter.

conceptPanel.heading: What Tarrowby has set up
conceptPanel.text: On Tarrowby's side: the laptops carry a VPN that connects by itself (Tarrowby Connect), every phone, tablet and laptop is encrypted and can be locked or wiped remotely, and the 24/7 service desk can sort a lost device the moment you ring. These are set up for you; your part is to keep the device with you and ring straight away if it goes missing.
